opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest one for me is coding. I spend a lot of my day writing code, and the models have gotten to the point where they're a real collaborator rather than a fancy autocomplete. If I need to write a script to analyze some results, or I'm working in a part of the codebase I don't know well, I can just describe what I want and get a working first draft, then iterate on it. Something that might have taken me an hour of looking up documentation and fiddling with syntax now takes a few minutes. And it changes what I'm willing to attempt. There are a lot of small things I wouldn't have bothered doing before because the effort wasn't worth it, and now they're cheap enough that I just do them.

Beyond coding, I use it a lot as a kind of thinking partner. If I'm trying to understand a paper in an area I'm less familiar with, I'll ask it to explain the key ideas, or I'll ask follow-up questions that would feel too basic to ask a colleague. It's very patient. I also find it useful for writing, not so much having it write things for me, but getting feedback on a draft, asking whether an argument is clear, or what objections someone might raise.

There's also a fun personal side. I've used it for things like planning trips or figuring out what's going on with some household problem. But if I had to pick one place where it's made the most practical difference, it's definitely programming. It's genuinely changed how I work day to day.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that when coding, they can describe what they want and get a working first draft of the code, clearly conveying that a natural-language description can be turned into code.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the place I get the most practical benefit is coding. I probably spend a big chunk of my day working with Claude on code at this point. It's not that it's writing entire systems for me end to end, although it's getting closer to that. It's more that there's a huge amount of work in engineering that is tedious but not actually hard, and the model just takes that off my plate. Writing boilerplate, converting something from one format to another, writing tests, figuring out why some obscure error is happening in a library I've never looked at before. Things where I know exactly what I want, and the bottleneck is just typing it out or looking up the right API.

The other thing I'd highlight is that it changes which tasks I'm even willing to start. There are a lot of small analyses or scripts that I used to think, "that would take me an hour, I'm not going to bother." Now it's ten minutes, so I just do it. And I think that's where a lot of the value is, not in doing the stuff you were already going to do faster, but in the long tail of things that previously weren't worth the effort.

Outside of coding, I use it a lot for just learning things quickly. If I'm reading a paper outside my area and there's a concept I don't understand, I'll ask about it the way I'd ask a knowledgeable coworker. It's really good at meeting you where you are and explaining at the right level. And for writing, it's great as a first-pass editor, where I'll paste in a draft and ask what's unclear or where I'm being sloppy.

The caveat I'd add is that it's still worth staying skeptical. I generally find it most useful in areas where I can quickly verify the output. With code, I run the tests and I know whether it worked. With a factual question in a domain I don't know, I have to be more careful. But that gap has been shrinking pretty fast, and that's one of the things that makes working on these models interesting, because the thing I use every day is very much the thing I'm working on.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes using AI for coding tasks such as boilerplate, tests, and API lookup, but does not clearly state that a plain English description of desired software behavior can be turned into implementing code.

astra-6.text:
For me, it’s mostly in coding. If I’m working in an unfamiliar part of a codebase, or using a library I don’t know very well, it’s useful to have something I can ask questions of as I go. That can save a lot of time searching through documentation.

The other thing is getting a first pass at an idea. I can say, “Here’s what I’m trying to do. What are a few ways I could approach it?” I still have to check the answer, but it gives me something concrete to react to, and that often helps me get unstuck.
